text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--Shareholders on the Copenhagen Stock Exchange saw the combined value of their holdings rise by 121 billion crowns to a total 620 billion during the first half of 1997, a 24 percent gain. Bond prices increased by 67 billion crowns to 1,878 billion, a 3.7 percent rise.
--Justice Minister Frank Jensen is heading into a political storm over his intervention with regional officials on the child-visitation provisions of his brother's divorce.

--Denmark's civil engineering industry faces crisis in a couple of years when the current crop of major infrastructure projects are completed a survey says, recommending that a planned overhaul of the railways be brought foward, to take up the slack.
--Danish businesses trading in China fear tough sanctions if the government continues to criticise Beijing's human-rights record, a study by stockbroker Carnegie shows.
--Norwegian shipping line Eidsiva has been authorised to begin ferry services between Roedby, Denmark and Puttgarden, Germany, breaking Danish state-owned Scandlines' monopoly.
--Unibank says that growth in private spending, about three percent a year, is strong "but not alarming".

--British cut-price air company Debonair plans to launch flights between Gothernburg, Sweden, and other European capitals. It also tends to make a public offering, to raise capital for further expansion.

--Carlsberg is to dismiss about half the 3,900 employees of its British Carlsberg-Tetley unit following the British government's ruling that it may not sell the company to British partner Bass and that Bass must sell its existing 50 percent stake in the firm.
--Denmark is unlikely to raise interest rates unless inflation reaches a level at which it weakens the crown currency, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell says. REUTER
